intro: This guide explains the grammar labels and word-class codes used in the dictionary. The explanations are short and designed for learners.

wordClasses.name: noun
wordClasses.summary: A word for a person, place, thing, or idea.
wordClasses.notes: Nouns can be countable, uncountable, or both.

wordClasses.name: verb
wordClasses.summary: A word for an action, event, or state.
wordClasses.notes: Verbs can be transitive, intransitive, or both.

wordClasses.name: adjective
wordClasses.summary: A word that describes a noun or pronoun.
wordClasses.notes: Some adjectives are gradable; others are not.

wordClasses.name: adverb
wordClasses.summary: A word that describes a verb, adjective, adverb, or whole sentence.
wordClasses.notes: Adverbs often answer how, when, where, or how much.

wordClasses.name: preposition
wordClasses.summary: A word that shows relation, such as place, time, or direction.
wordClasses.notes: Prepositions are usually followed by a noun or pronoun.

wordClasses.name: conjunction
wordClasses.summary: A word that connects words, phrases, or clauses.
wordClasses.notes: Coordinating conjunctions join equal parts; subordinating conjunctions join dependent clauses.

wordClasses.name: determiner
wordClasses.summary: A word used before a noun to show which one, how many, or whose.
wordClasses.notes: Articles, possessives, and quantifiers are determiners.

wordClasses.name: pronoun
wordClasses.summary: A word used instead of a noun or noun phrase.
wordClasses.notes: Pronouns can be subject, object, possessive, reflexive, or indefinite.

wordClasses.name: interjection
wordClasses.summary: A short word or sound that shows feeling or reaction.

wordClasses.name: numeral
wordClasses.summary: A word or symbol that expresses a number or order.
wordClasses.notes: Cardinals show quantity; ordinals show order.

wordClasses.name: phrase
wordClasses.summary: A group of words that acts as a single unit.
wordClasses.notes: Phrases can have meanings that are not obvious from each word alone.

wordClasses.name: abbreviation
wordClasses.summary: A short form of a word or phrase.
wordClasses.notes: Abbreviations may be spoken as letters or as words.

grammarCodes.meaning: countable noun: it has singular and plural forms
uncountable noun: it usually has no plural form
noun that can be countable or uncountable depending on meaning
transitive verb: it takes a direct object
intransitive verb: it does not take a direct object
verb that can be transitive or intransitive
grammarCodes.example: The door opened. / She opened the door.

grammarCodes.meaning: adjective that can be weaker or stronger
adjective that usually does not take degrees
adjective used after a linking verb

grammarCodes.example: an asleep child is unusual; a sleeping child is normal

grammarCodes.meaning: noun usually used in singular form
noun usually used in plural form
used in careful, official, or academic situations

sections.title: Articles
body: English uses 'a' or 'an' for non-specific singular countable nouns, and 'the' for specific or known nouns.
Use 'an' before a vowel sound, not just a vowel letter.

sections.title: Countability
body: Countable nouns can be counted and have plural forms.
Uncountable nouns refer to mass, abstract ideas, or substances and usually do not take a/an or a plural -s.

sections.title: Verb patterns
body: Some verbs take an object, some do not, and some can do both.
Learners should notice patterns such as verb + to-infinitive, verb + -ing, and verb + object + infinitive.

sections.title: Comparatives and superlatives
body: Short adjectives often add -er and -est. Longer adjectives usually use more and most.
Irregular forms must be learned separately.

sections.title: Prepositions
body: Prepositions often show place, time, movement, or relationship.
Many preposition choices are fixed by common usage, so they should be learned in phrases.

sections.title: Word order
body: A basic English statement usually follows subject + verb + object order.
Questions often change word order or use an auxiliary verb.

sections.title: Punctuation
body: Punctuation helps readers see sentence boundaries, pauses, and meaning.
Apostrophes show possession or contractions, but they do not form ordinary plurals.

sections.title: Register and region
body: Register labels show whether a word is neutral, formal, informal, slang, or offensive.
Region labels such as BrE, AmE, and AusE show where a word or spelling is most common.

sections.title: Common learner errors
body: Learners often confuse countable and uncountable nouns, omit articles, or choose the wrong preposition.
Checking grammar codes and examples helps avoid these mistakes.
